title: Secrets Access Project
summary: Final project of the Express section: build a password-gated page. A form posts a password to /check; the correct one reveals secret.html, a wrong one returns the user to the home page. A walkthrough shows a middleware-based solution.

concepts.heading: Project structure
points: Starter folder: an empty index.js (all code goes here) and a public folder with two pre-built pages: index.html (h1 plus a password form) and secret.html (the protected content).
Dependencies are body-parser and express. Running node solution.js without having run npm i gives ERR_MODULE_NOT_FOUND.
Inspect the form first: its action is /check, method POST, and the password input's name attribute is password. That name is the key to read from req.body.

concepts.heading: How the solution works
points: Imports express, body-parser, dirname and fileURLToPath, then rebuilds __dirname exactly as in earlier lessons. These lines can be copied from earlier projects; the point is to understand them, not memorise them.
A flag variable userIsAuthorised starts as false.
app.use(bodyParser.urlencoded({ extended: true })) comes first so req.body exists.

passwordCheck(req, res, next) is a custom middleware: it reads req.body['password'], compares it to the secret, sets the flag to true on a match, and always calls next(). Putting the check in middleware is a design choice, treating it as authorisation before the handler; doing it inside the route handler is equally valid.
POST /check sends public/secret.html if authorised; otherwise it sends the home page again or calls res.redirect('/').
res.redirect(url) tells the browser to go to another URL, giving a shorter way to return the user to the home page.

Express now bundles the urlencoded parser, so app.use(express.urlencoded({ extended: true })) replaces body-parser with no extra package. The instructor keeps body-parser because it is what most online code uses and it names what is happening.

concepts.heading: Learning advice given
points: Try the project before looking at the solution; struggling is how the skill sticks.
Programming is about knowing where to look things up, not memorising syntax.

task.name: Secrets Access Project
task.starting_point: Extracted Secrets Project zip: blank index.js, public/index.html (password form posting to /check), public/secret.html.
task.goal: Home page shows the form. Submitting the correct password shows secret.html; a wrong password sends the user back to the home page.
steps: cd into the project and run npm i (express and body-parser).
Read index.html and note the form action (/check), method (POST) and input name (password).
In index.js import express, body-parser and the path/url helpers; set up __dirname, app and port 3000.
Add the urlencoded body parser middleware.
Write a middleware (or inline check) that compares req.body.password to your chosen secret and records the result; end with next().
Add POST /check that sends secret.html when authorised, otherwise redirects or re-sends index.html.
Add app.listen, run with node index.js or nodemon, and test right and wrong passwords at localhost:3000.
task.expected_result: Correct password: the secrets list page. Wrong password: back at the Secrets home page with the form.
task.reference_repo_path: Section 24 - Express.js with Node.js/24.05 - Secrets Access Project/solution.js

pitfalls: Wrong name attribute: req.body key must match the input's name.
Declaring the body parser after the password middleware, so req.body is undefined.
(Extra) The solution's userIsAuthorised flag is global and never resets, so after one correct login every later request, from any user, counts as authorised. A per-request check avoids this.
(Extra) Sending a password in plain text with a text input is fine for a demo only; real apps use type=password, HTTPS and hashing.

Reference repo note: its index.js is a student's variant (password constant checked inside the route, repeated app.use lines at the end, no app.listen); solution.js is the one matching the lecture. Ignore the author footers in the HTML.
